meta.title: When the CEO Is the Weak Link: How Founders Limit Growth in Nigeria
meta.description: In many Nigerian companies, the biggest risk to growth is not the economy or the competition. It is the person at the top. Here is how to spot it, and what to do about it.
meta.image_alt: A business leader in a navy blue native outfit stands thoughtfully at his office window overlooking a city bridge, while his staff wait together in a glass-walled office behind him.

title: When the CEO Is the Weak Link
dek: Every business owner spends hours studying the market, the competition, and the customer. But only a few spend the same hours studying themselves. Yet in many companies across Nigeria today, the biggest risk to growth is not the economy or the competition. It is the person at the top.

paragraphs: This is not an easy thing to say to a founder who has poured years into building something from nothing. But it needs saying, because a company can only grow as far as its leader is willing to grow with it.

According to the International Labour Organization (ILO), SMEs make up 96 percent of all businesses in Nigeria, provide 84 percent of employment, and contribute 48 percent of the country's GDP. Yet reports cited in the Nigerian press, including a 2022 report from fintech company Kippa, estimate that about 80 percent of businesses in Africa fail within five years of starting. This means that simply surviving that stretch of time already puts a business ahead of most others that started around the same time. Beyond survival, whether the company grows or remains stagnant in one place often comes down to the person running it.

sections.heading: Understand How It Starts
paragraphs: When you walk into many small and mid-sized businesses, you will notice a pattern of stiff control. The owner still approves every purchase order, no matter how small. Every hire waits for their final nod. Every client email passes through their inbox before it goes out. On the surface, this looks like discipline. In reality, it is a bottleneck wearing the costume of leadership.

sections.text: When a business cannot function for a single day without its owner physically present, that business does not have a strong leader. It has a single point of failure.

paragraphs: The same pattern shows up in decision making. Talented staff raise a concern, but once they are ignored more times than they can count, they stop raising it. The business loses the insight and nobody notices.

sections.heading: Why Founders Never See It Coming
paragraphs: Most founders built their companies by trusting their own instincts and gut feeling, often against advice from people who told them the idea would never work. That instinct served them well early on and gave them the extra kick to make things work against all odds. The trouble starts when the company outgrows what one person can carry, and the founder keeps leading exactly as they did on day one.

Success early on can convince a leader that their way is the only way and that everyone must do things in the exact sequence. Some founders have created a culture where junior staff hesitate to challenge them, and the founder can go years without hearing one piece of feedback that would change everything.

sections.heading: What This Costs the Business
paragraphs: A company led this way pays a quiet but steady price. Skilled employees will leave after getting tired of decisions made without their input. Promising opportunities will stall because they sit on a desk waiting for a signature that takes days to come. Managers will stop managing and start waiting, because they know the real decisions happen elsewhere.

A survey carried out by Gallup found that a manager accounts for at least 70 percent of the difference in how engaged employees feel at work. In a founder-led business, also known as a one-man business, the founder is that manager for the whole company. Every hesitation to trust a manager, every ignored suggestion, and every decision pulled back to the top ripples through engagement long before it shows up in a resignation letter.

These actions do not affect company growth immediately. They eat the company from the inside out, while the CEO, who was supposedly expected to be the strongest link, watches the rot set in. Issues pile up and show up months later in the form of missed targets nobody can fully explain and staff turnover that keeps repeating for reasons nobody wants to say out loud.

sections.heading: How To Stop Being The Weak Link
paragraphs: The fix to this founder-led problem does not require you to step back completely or hand over control you are not ready to release. It starts smaller: pick one decision this month that does not need to pass through you, and let a manager own it fully, mistakes included.

It also means asking a direct question in meetings and waiting for the answer, rather than waiting for a pause to speak. It does not matter if the response fails to meet your expectation at first. If you sense a gap in their intelligence, get them up to speed with trainings, management books, and/or external consulting to sharpen their minds. The goal is for you, the founder, to gradually become the least intelligent in the room, not by diminishing yourself, but by constantly improving others to their full potential. Over time, staff learn whether their opinions matter by watching what happens after they share one, not by what is written in the handbook.

Founders who make this shift often notice something unexpected. The business speeds up when they step back from daily decisions, because the people closest to the work finally have room to do it well.

sections.heading: The Real Measure of Leadership
paragraphs: A strong CEO builds a team capable of finding answers without them in the room, rather than trying to hold every answer alone. That difference decides whether a business depends on one person or lasts well beyond them.

entries.q: How do I know if I am the weak link in my own company?
entries.a: A useful test is whether the business can function for a full day without you physically available. If every purchase, hire, or client email still has to pass through you, or if managers have stopped raising concerns because they have been overruled before, those are signs that decisions are bottlenecking at the top rather than being distributed to the people equipped to make them.

entries.q: What is a single point of failure in a business?
entries.a: A single point of failure is any role or person the business cannot operate without, even briefly. When a founder personally approves every decision, no matter how small, the entire company's output depends on that one person's availability. A resilient business spreads authority so that operations continue smoothly even when any one person, including the founder, is unavailable.

entries.q: How does founder over-involvement affect staff engagement?
entries.a: According to Gallup research, a manager accounts for at least 70 percent of the difference in how engaged their team feels at work. In a founder-led business, the founder is effectively that manager for the whole company. When feedback is ignored and decisions are consistently pulled back to the top, engagement erodes well before it shows up as a resignation, usually appearing first as missed targets and unexplained turnover.

entries.q: How can a founder start delegating without losing control of the business?
entries.a: Start small rather than stepping back all at once. Pick one recurring decision this month that does not need to pass through you, and let a manager own it completely, including the mistakes that come with it. Pair that with genuinely waiting for answers in meetings rather than filling the silence yourself. Staff learn whether their input matters by watching what happens after they give it, not from what is written in a handbook.
